idiom_name: extension methods returning the next sequence (Where/Select) and `this`-returning builder methods
implementation_notes: C# makes the fluent chain an ordinary part of the language: extension methods let a fluent surface be attached to any type without modifying it, and the LINQ standard query operators (Where, Select, OrderBy, GroupBy) are exactly such a chain over IEnumerable<T>/IQueryable<T>, with query syntax compiled into these very calls. Mutable chains are written the everyday way - `public Foo WithX(...) { ...; return this; }` as in StringBuilder.Append and the IHostBuilder/WebApplicationBuilder configuration chains - while query-like APIs return a new sequence per step. What replaces the classic structure: for queries, extension methods keep the fluent grammar outside the data type, and C# 9 covariant return types let a derived builder return its own type without overriding every step. Prefer expression-bodied, value-returning steps for shared queries and reserve a receiver-returning builder for assembling one object.
code_sketch:
var request = new HttpRequestBuilder()
    .WithMethod("POST")
    .WithTimeout(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10))
    .Build();                          // terminal: validates once

var names = people
    .Where(p => p.Age > 18)            // extension method: IEnumerable<Person> -> IEnumerable<Person>
    .OrderBy(p => p.Name)
    .Select(p => p.Name);
pitfalls: Deferred execution: the chain records steps and runs when enumerated, so mutating the source or enumerating twice silently re-runs (or re-queries) the pipeline; call ToList()/ToArray() to make the result stable.

A `this`-returning mutating method on a class is indistinguishable at the call site from an extension-method chain that returns new values, so two variables taken from the same base builder alias one object; document mutability and prefer immutable steps for shared APIs.

Before C# 9 a builder method inherited from a base class returned the base type and the chain lost its derived steps; without covariant return types the fluent surface for a hierarchy must be reshaped or every step overridden.
